\paragraph{Text classifiers and LLM annotation.}
\citet{grimmer2022} and \citet{feder_etal2022} provide foundations for text-as-data and causal inference in NLP. \citet{wood_doughty2018} first applied DAG reasoning to classifier error; \citet{teblunthuis2024} gave the most complete binary treatment ($K{=}2$, four DAGs); \citet{lee_wood_doughty2024} extended to categorical LLM classifiers but covered only confounding. On annotation quality, \citet{gilardi2023chatgpt} and \citet{ziems2024can} document the rapid adoption of LLM annotators (surveyed by \citealt{tan2024llm}), \citet{baumann2025} found 31\% incorrect conclusions, \citet{pangakis_wolken_fasching2023} demonstrated that automated annotations require task-specific validation, \citet{cheng_mayya_sedoc2024} propose structured approaches to reduce LLM measurement error, \citet{variance_aware_llm2026} develop variance-aware annotation protocols, \citet{hidden_measurement_error2026} characterizes hidden measurement error in LLM pipelines, and \citet{kim_garg2025} showed 60\% error correlation across models. \citet{audinet2025} benchmark debiasing; \citet{keith_jensen_oconnor2020} survey the broader landscape. These works either restrict to binary labels, cover a single topology, or diagnose quality without connecting it to causal validity.

lines: Foundations appear in \citet{carroll2006, gustafson2004, buonaccorsi2010, bound2001measurement}, with DAG-based formalization by \citet{hernan_cole2009} and \citet{kuroki_pearl2014}. For binary variables, non-differential misclassification biases toward the null~\cite{brenner1993, ogburn_vanderweele2012}, but this fails for polytomous exposures~\cite{dosemeci1990, jurek2005, veirod_laake2001}. Extensions address differential measurement error~\cite{edwards_lessler_naimi2021, imai_yamamoto2010}, endogenous misreporting~\cite{nguimkeu_denteh_tchernis2019}, mismeasured covariates under IPW~\cite{shu_yi2019a, shu_yi2019b}, mediation with mismeasured mediators~\cite{valeri_vanderweele2013}, nonclassical error~\cite{schennach2020mismeasured}, and multiply robust estimation~\cite{wei2025multiply}. All analyze a single DAG topology; ours characterizes how the \emph{same} confusion matrix produces qualitatively different bias across seven topologies.

On annotation quality, \citet{gilardi2023chatgpt} and \citet{ziems2024can} document rapid LLM annotator adoption (surveyed by \citealt{tan2024llm}), \citet{baumann2025} found 31\% incorrect conclusions, and \citet{kim_garg2025} showed 60\% error correlation across models~\cite{pangakis_wolken_fasching2023, cheng_mayya_sedoc2024, variance_aware_llm2026, hidden_measurement_error2026}. \citet{audinet2025} benchmark debiasing; \citet{keith_jensen_oconnor2020} survey the landscape. These works either restrict to binary labels, cover a single topology, or diagnose quality without connecting it to causal validity.
\paragraph{Sensitivity analysis and correction methods.}

Our ASV framework draws on the sensitivity analysis without assumptions of \citet{ding_vanderweele2016}, E-values~\cite{vanderweele_ding2017, mathur2018}, the robustness value of \citet{cinelli2020making}, and the mediation sensitivity analysis of \citet{imai_keele_yamamoto2010}, and text-based causal inference methods~\cite{pryzant_etal2021}, but parametrizes annotation error severity rather than omitted variable strength or sequential ignorability violations. The quantitative bias analysis framework of \citet{lash2009} provides a complementary epidemiologic perspective, and \citet{mahajan2006} establishes identification of regression models with misclassified regressors via instrumental variables. The unified measurement-error and missing-data framework of \citet{blackwell_honaker_king2017} similarly motivates treating annotation noise as a first-class object of inference. For correction, PPI++~\cite{angelopoulos2023} and DSL~\cite{egami_hinck_stewart_wei2023} are topology-agnostic; \citet{zrnic_candes2024} extend PPI to gold-free settings, \citet{demirel2024prediction} generalize prediction-powered inference to causal parameters across populations, and \citet{cadei2025} adapt it to treatment-effect targets via a deconfounded risk objective, and \citet{gligoric2025} leverage LLM confidence scores. Our contribution reveals that this agnosticism is costly: correction effectiveness is itself topology-dependent, with matrix-based methods provably ineffective for four topologies. Bayesian measurement error models~\cite{richardson1993bayesian, gustafson2004} and EM imputation offer alternatives that bypass FWL invariance.

\begin{remark}[ASV and E-values as complementary tools]
\label{rem:evalue}
ASV diagnostics and E-values~\cite{vanderweele_ding2017} address different bias sources---annotation error vs.\ unmeasured confounding---and are most valuable when used jointly (Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity_comparison}, Appendix).
\emph{(i)~Topology dependence}: ASV captures how the same $C$ has different consequences across topologies; E-values are topology-agnostic.
\emph{(ii)~Sign-flip diagnostic}: sign-flip ASV $\delta^*_{\mathrm{sf}}$ targets a failure mode absent from unmeasured confounding.
\emph{(iii)~Parametric structure}: ASV searches $C(\delta)$ paths in the column-stochastic polytope; E-values optimize over $[1,\infty)$.
\end{remark}

Under alternating-sign effects ($\boldsymbol{\beta}{=}[0,\,1.0,\,-0.5]$), magnitude ASV is 0.09 for exposure, 0.20 for IV, 0.35 for confounding, and $\infty$ for M-bias (Table~\ref{tab:asv_stability})---the same annotator quality produces a $4{\times}$ difference in tolerable error, determined entirely by DAG topology. This topology-dependent diagnostic is unavailable in E-value frameworks, which treat all confounding structures identically.

For $K{=}2$, Theorem~\ref{thm:monotone} guarantees exact monotonicity; for $K{\geq}3$, monotonicity rests on numerical evidence (Conjecture~\ref{conj:monotone}). Sign-flip ASV $< 1$ flags sign-reversal-prone pairs; magnitude ASV $< \delta_{\text{observed}}$ indicates bias exceeds tolerance (Algorithm~\ref{alg:correction}). The safe/fragile partition is stable across DGP parameterizations; within-group ordering depends on coefficient structure (Appendix~\ref{sec:asv_stability}). Under moderate effect sizes ($|\beta| \leq 1$), the worst-case monotonicity deviation ($\varepsilon < 0.02$ for non-exposure, $\varepsilon < 0.08$ for exposure) is small relative to inter-topology ASV gaps (spanning 0.09 to $\infty$), ensuring that the vulnerability ranking is robust.

80	We evaluate five correction methods (naive plug-in, MLA, DSL~\cite{egami_hinck_stewart_wei2023}, MC-SIMEX, PPI++~\cite{angelopoulos2023}) across all topologies (210 configurations; Table~\ref{tab:correction}, Appendix~\ref{app:supplementary}).
81	
82	\paragraph{FWL invariance.}
83	Under linear OLS, FWL implies that any linear transformation of $\mathbf{D}^*$ preserves the column space relative to $T$ for the four covariate topologies, so naive plug-in and MLA achieve exactly 0.0\% bias reduction (Appendix~\ref{app:fwl_proof}); exposure and IV are excluded. Under logistic regression, FWL invariance breaks and matrix corrections achieve non-zero bias reduction, though the safe/fragile partition is preserved ($|\Delta\,\text{SF}_\tau| < 0.02$; Appendix~\ref{sec:logistic_dgp},~\ref{sec:fwl_nonlinear}).
84

10	We address these gaps with three contributions:
11	
12	\begin{enumerate}
13	\item \textbf{Multi-class bias taxonomy.} We derive bias expressions for seven canonical DAG topologies\footnote{These span the four structural roles of the annotated variable: treatment (exposure), outcome-side covariate (confounding, mediation, M-bias, front-door), selection variable (collider), and instrument (IV).} (Figure~\ref{fig:dag_taxonomy}) under $K$-class non-differential misclassification, establishing a sign-preservation/reversal dichotomy: five topologies preserve the treatment effect sign, while exposure and IV can reverse it (binarization amplifies this gap $154{\times}$; Appendix~\ref{app:binarization}).
14	
15	\item \textbf{Annotation Sensitivity Values.} Building on the bias taxonomy, we define three ASV diagnostics---magnitude, significance, and sign-flip---with proved envelope monotonicity for $K{=}2$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:monotone}) and empirically validated $\varepsilon$-approximate monotonicity for $K{\geq}3$ (Conjecture~\ref{conj:monotone}, $\varepsilon < 0.02$ under moderate effects). These reveal a vulnerability spectrum from IV (maximally fragile) to M-bias (immune, ASV $= \infty$), enabling topology-specific error tolerance assessment.
16	
17	\item \textbf{Correction guidance.} As a practical implication, we evaluate five correction methods and prove an FWL invariance result: matrix-based corrections achieve exactly 0\% bias reduction for four covariate topologies, meaning confusion-matrix inversion fails silently for most causal designs.
18	\end{enumerate}
19

10	Our analysis characterizes systematic bias---the value an estimator converges to as $N \to \infty$ (the probability limit, or plim)---rather than finite-sample variance. The Frisch--Waugh--Lovell (FWL) theorem guarantees that each regression coefficient equals the coefficient from a simple regression after residualizing all other variables; this is why matrix-based corrections fail for covariate topologies (Section~\ref{sec:correction}): replacing the mismeasured variable with a corrected version does not change the residualized relationship. The Wald estimator (ratio of reduced-form to first-stage effects) diverges under weak instruments; Dirichlet priors over probability vectors represent uncertainty over misclassification patterns. Table~\ref{tab:notation} (Appendix~\ref{app:notation_table}) collects all notation.
11	
12	\begin{definition}[Non-differential misclassification]
13	\label{def:nondiff}
14	Misclassification of $A$ is non-differential with respect to outcome $Y$ and covariates $\mathbf{Z}$ if $P(A^*{=}j \mid A{=}k, Y, \mathbf{Z}) = P(A^*{=}j \mid A{=}k) = C_{jk}$ for all $j,k$.
15	\end{definition}
16	
17	This holds when the LLM classifies without observing the outcome---the typical CSS setup~\cite{ziems2024can}; topic-stratified confusion matrices confirm cross-group stability (Appendix~\ref{sec:nondiff_verify}). Violations arise when pretraining data encodes $A$--$Y$ associations; our stress test (Appendix~\ref{sec:nondiff_stress}) shows $<$3~pp degradation under uniform $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ violations, but $\varepsilon{=}0.01$ structured departure produces sign reversal in 14/16 $K{\geq}3$ exposure configurations (Appendix~\ref{sec:realistic_epsilon}). Practitioners can test this by comparing $C$ across outcome strata; in typical CSS pipelines where annotation is performed without access to $Y$, non-differentiality is structurally ensured~\cite{ziems2024can}.
18	
19	We study seven canonical DAG topologies (Figure~\ref{fig:dag_taxonomy})~\cite{pearl2009, hernan2020causal} in which $A$ occupies structurally distinct causal roles: confounder, exposure, mediator, collider, M-bias variable, front-door mediator, and instrument. Throughout, we derive probability limits under \emph{linear} structural equation models~\cite{carroll2006}, the standard framework for exact characterization of topology-dependent bias; robustness under logistic regression~\cite{stefanski_carroll1985} is verified in Appendix~\ref{sec:logistic_dgp} and~\ref{sec:fwl_nonlinear}.
20	
21	\subsection{Multi-Class Bias Expressions}
22	\label{sec:bias_expressions}

12 个 LLM configs × 3 Y-proxies = 36 permutation tests (B=10,000)：
- **Content-independent Y (text_length)**: 1/12 rejection at α=0.05（符合预期假阳性率），median p=0.508
- **Content-dependent Y (topic)**: 11/12 rejection（预期：LLM 观测文本内容）

在 appendix_proofs.tex 的 sign reversal determinants (§B.24, L1419) 之后、Notation (L1421) 之前，插入：

```latex
\subsection{Y-Stratified Non-Differential Verification}
\label{sec:y_stratified_test}

We directly test the non-differential assumption (Definition~\ref{def:nondiff}) by stratifying confusion matrices by outcome-proxy variables and testing $C(Y{=}\text{high}) \approx C(Y{=}\text{low})$. Using 12 LLM configurations on VAST ($K{=}3$; 4 models $\times$ 3 prompting strategies, 1{,}500 samples each), we compute per-stratum confusion matrices under three Y-proxies and apply permutation tests ($B{=}10{,}000$, test statistic: $\max_{j,k} |C^{(0)}_{jk} - C^{(1)}_{jk}|$).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Y-stratified non-differential test. Content-independent Y (text length) shows no significant violation (1/12 rejection $\approx$ expected false positive rate at $\alpha{=}0.05$). Content-dependent proxies (topic, sentiment) show expected violations since LLMs observe text content.}
\label{tab:y_stratified}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Y proxy} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Reject ($\alpha{=}0.05$)} & \textbf{Median $p$} \\
\midrule
Text length & Content-indep. & 1/12 & 0.508 \\
Topic & Content-dep. & 11/12 & 0.002 \\
Sentiment & Content-dep. & 10/12 & 0.014 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The single text-length rejection (Llama-4 few-shot-3, $p{=}0.027$) is consistent with the expected false positive rate ($0.05 \times 12 = 0.6$). Content-dependent proxies (topic, sentiment) show systematic rejection because LLMs process text content from which these variables can be inferred, violating $Y \perp \text{text} \mid A$. In causal inference applications, $Y$ is typically an external outcome (e.g., health status, economic indicator) that cannot be inferred from the annotated text, satisfying the independence condition. The content-dependent rejections confirm statistical power: the test can detect violations when they exist.
```


For $K \geq 3$, the determinant of $C$ is the strongest single predictor: $\det(C) < 0.014$ identifies sign-reversing matrices with 100\% specificity (zero false positives) and 85.7\% sensitivity. An AND rule combining $\min_k C_{kk} < 0.55$ with mean column entropy $> 0.40$ achieves 100\% sensitivity at 88.9\% specificity. These rules are robust to $\beta$-scaling (accuracy unchanged at $0.3{\times}$ and $3{\times}$ effect magnitude) but sensitive to $\beta$-sign structure: under uniform-positive $\beta$ (all coefficients same sign), no matrices produce sign reversal regardless of $C$, as cancellation across differently-signed coefficients is the underlying mechanism.
+\subsection{Y-Stratified Non-Differential Verification}
+\label{sec:y_stratified_test}

+We directly test the non-differential assumption (Definition~\ref{def:nondiff}) by stratifying confusion matrices by outcome-proxy variables and testing $C(Y{=}\text{high}) \approx C(Y{=}\text{low})$. Using 12 LLM configurations on VAST ($K{=}3$; 4 models $\times$ 3 prompting strategies, 1{,}500 samples each), we compute per-stratum confusion matrices under three Y-proxies and apply permutation tests ($B{=}10{,}000$, test statistic: $\max_{j,k} |C^{(0)}_{jk} - C^{(1)}_{jk}|$).
+\begin{table}[h]
+\centering
+\small

+\caption{Y-stratified non-differential test. Content-independent Y (text length) shows no significant violation (1/12 rejection $\approx$ expected false positive rate at $\alpha{=}0.05$). Content-dependent proxies (topic, sentiment) show expected violations since LLMs observe text content.}
+\label{tab:y_stratified}
+\begin{tabular}{lccc}
+\toprule
+\textbf{Y proxy} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Reject ($\alpha{=}0.05$)} & \textbf{Median $p$} \\
+\midrule
+Text length & Content-indep. & 1/12 & 0.508 \\
+Topic & Content-dep. & 11/12 & 0.002 \\
+Sentiment & Content-dep. & 10/12 & 0.014 \\
+\bottomrule
+\end{tabular}
+\end{table}

+The single text-length rejection (Llama-4 few-shot-3, $p{=}0.027$) is consistent with the expected false positive rate ($0.05 \times 12 = 0.6$). Content-dependent proxies (topic, sentiment) show systematic rejection because LLMs process text content from which these variables can be inferred, violating $Y \perp \text{text} \mid A$. In causal inference applications, $Y$ is typically an external outcome (e.g., health status, economic indicator) that cannot be inferred from the annotated text, satisfying the independence condition. The content-dependent rejections confirm statistical power: the test can detect violations when they exist.
